title: Power from the Wind
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: People have used the wind for thousands of years, to sail ships and to grind grain. Today the same force is used to make electricity. A wind turbine turns the energy of moving air into power for homes, factories and schools, without burning any fuel or producing any smoke. Wind is one of the fastest-growing sources of energy in the world, and in some countries, such as Denmark, it already supplies about half of the electricity. This passage explains how a turbine works, where they are built and what problems the technology still has to solve.

A modern turbine looks like a tall white tower with three long blades. When the wind blows, the blades, which are shaped like the wings of an aeroplane, are pushed round, turning a shaft inside a housing at the top of the tower, called the nacelle. The shaft is connected to a gearbox, which increases the slow turning of the blades, about fifteen revolutions a minute, to the much faster turning, over a thousand revolutions a minute, that a generator needs. The generator produces electricity, which passes through a transformer and then travels along cables to the grid. Sensors measure the direction of the wind, and motors turn the whole nacelle to face it.

Size matters. The power in the wind rises very rapidly with its speed: if the wind speed doubles, the power increases eight times. Taller towers reach higher, where the wind is stronger and steadier, and longer blades sweep a larger area. A typical turbine today may stand a hundred metres high, with blades fifty metres long, and a single machine can supply electricity to well over a thousand homes. The largest sea-based turbines are even bigger, taller than a fifty-storey building, with blades that can be as long as a football pitch.

The best places for wind farms are those where the wind is strong and regular: coasts, open plains, mountain passes and the sea. Offshore wind farms have an advantage, as the wind at sea is stronger and more constant than that on land, and there are fewer people to disturb. But building at sea is more expensive, since the turbines must be fixed to the sea bed or float on platforms, and the repairs require boats. On land, wind farms are cheaper but may meet opposition from local residents, who object to the noise or to the appearance of tall machines on the horizon.

The most serious problem is that the wind does not blow all the time. On a calm day, a wind farm produces almost nothing, and on a stormy day, turbines must be stopped to prevent damage. The electricity grid has to be balanced from minute to minute, since supply must match demand, so other sources are needed to fill the gaps. Engineers are working on solutions: batteries to store extra power, networks that connect distant regions so that a calm place can borrow from a windy one, and better forecasts of the weather. Another solution is to use surplus electricity to make hydrogen, which can be stored and burnt later.

Wind farms also affect wildlife. Birds and bats sometimes collide with the blades, although the number killed is much smaller than the number killed by cats, buildings or cars. Careful planning can reduce the risk: turbines are kept away from migration routes and nesting sites, and some are stopped for a short time when radar shows that a flock is approaching. Noise is another complaint, though a modern turbine at a distance of three hundred metres is no louder than a quiet conversation. Dr Fiona Maxwell, an environmental scientist, concludes that the harm caused by wind power is small when compared with the damage caused by coal and oil.

Many governments plan to expand wind power rapidly. Countries with large open spaces, including several in Central Asia, are building wind farms on plains and deserts where winds blow strongly for most of the year. Turbines are becoming more efficient and cheaper, and the cost of electricity from a good wind farm is now lower than that of a new coal or gas power station in many regions. Dr Maxwell believes that wind will supply a quarter of the world's electricity within a generation, provided that the grids and storage keep pace. She adds that the greatest change must be in attitudes, since people must accept that producing energy is a visible activity, which cannot be hidden.
